Title: "The Houston Kid": Great Songwriter Mines His Past, Strikes Gold
Chunks: 0,1,2
It’s ironic. In 1988, the country-music singer/songwriter Rodney Crowell released his fifth album, _Diamonds and Dirt_, which set a record, so to speak. No country album had ever spawned five #1 singles. _Diamonds and Dirt_ did, elevating the 38-year-old, who had written hits for artists from Waylon Jennings to Crystal Gayle and spent three years playing rhythm guitar in Emmylou Harris’s band, to the upper reaches of country-music stardom.
Artistically, the songs were nothing special, but with Columbia Records’ hitmaking machinery propelling them, they were catchy enough to top _Billboard_’s country chart. One, the driving, uptempo, and funny “She’s Crazy For Leaving,” was a legitimate #1. The rest were well-produced, well-marketed pablum.
Hence the irony I’ve alluded to. Crowell released his 10th album, _The Houston Kid_, in 2001, on little Sugar Hill Records (not to be confused with rap’s Sugar Hill). Evidently, the album had too little commercial potential to warrant a major label’s attention. No songs from _The Houston Kid_ charted. Yet critics—including this one, who reviewed the record for _Entertainment Weekly—_ almost unanimously agreed that this album was the artist’s finest piece of work yet, leaving Crowell’s major-label releases in the dirt.
One realizes on a first listen that _The Houston Kid_ is not the usual collection of 10 or so widely disparate songs. It’s what is known in the record business as a concept album, in this case an autobiographical song cycle, although, as anyone familiar with the contours of Crowell’s life recognized, _The Houston Kid_ made little attempt to stick to the facts. It was a work of imagination more or less based on the facts, and it was funny, sad, angry, ironic and deeply moving.
Crowell grew up on the wrong side of the tracks: run-down East Houston in the 1950s. Raunchy or not, the neighborhood had plenty to offer a lively kid with an appetite for fun and an imagination, as the opening song, “Telephone Road,” makes clear:
Video 11

“The Rock of My Soul,” which follows, is an unsparing portrait of the narrator’s parents, further establishing the harsh economic and emotional circumstances in which Crowell, or his persona, was raised, and the boy’s determination to avoid his mama and daddy’s fate.
Video 12
By the fifth song, “Wandering Boy,” the story has jumped ahead a number of years and taken a sharp turn onto an entirely imaginary road, about the brother Crowell never had (he was an only child), who, moreover, is dying of AIDs, and whom the protagonist urges to come home, where he can die comforted by a brother’s love. “Wandering Boy” is an unsentimental heartbreaker, strong evidence of Crowell’s growth as a writer since those late-‘80s Columbia hits.
Crowell had married into country-music royalty in 1979, tying the knot with Johnny Cash’s daughter Rosanne, a star herself. The couple divorced in 1992 but remained on friendly enough terms for Rosanne’s father not merely to agree to sing on _The Houston Kid_’s sixth song, “I Walk the Line (Revisited)”, but to sing a _rewritten version_ of “I Walk the Line”, allowing his ex-son-in-law to “paint a mustache on John’s Mona Lisa," as Crowell later put it. Cash good-naturedly throws himself into the spirit of Crowell’s brazen rewrite, singing the hell out of it. “I Walk the Line (Revisited)” is not only hilarious, but captures (most likely imagines) a major moment in the childhood of a future country-music singer.
Video 13
“Highway 17,” which immediately follows Crowell’s act of _lèse-majesté,_ packs quite an emotional wallop. The song’s narrator, presumably the Crowell character’s semi-hoodlum of a father, is a career thief with what he considers a master plan, who suffers agonizingly at what was to be his moment of triumph. “Highway 17” may be _The Houston Kid_’s most imaginative and visceral song. Here’s Crowell singing it live in 2010.
Video 14

Four songs follow “Highway 17,” all of them strong, especially “U Don’t Know How Much I Hate You,” with its jolting last-line confession. To these ears, the song could easily have been inspired by Crowell’s and Cash’s divorce. Even if it was written after Crowell’s 1998 remarriage, resentment lingers.
In the final song of the 11-song cycle, the narrator, amid peaceful circumstances at last, looks back on his melodrama of a life, forgives his now-departed parents their transgressions, and counts his blessings. The song is titled “Love is All I Need.” Here’s a performance from 2009.
Video 15
More than a dozen Crowell albums, including collaborations—two with his old boss Emmylou Harris—have followed _The Houston Kid._ There are many I haven’t listened to. All I can say is that at the time it was released, it was by far Crowell’s best piece of work. He has since collected many awards, both for lifetime achievement and individual songs and albums. Neither _The Houston Kid_ nor any of its songs were nominated for, let alone won, anything.
In 2011, Crowell published a memoir, _Chinaberry Sidewalks_ (Vintage), its title taken from the chinaberry branches with which Addie Cauzette Crowell regularly whipped her son. _Chinaberry Sidewalks_ makes it clear how many liberties Crowell took with the truth in _The Houston Kid_. Which, of course, detracts not a bit from the album’s achievement. _Chinaberry Sidewalks_ is a work of non-fiction (and a well-written one at that). _The Houston Kid_ is an imaginative reworking of Crowell’s past, sticking to fact when it serves his purposes, and altering it, or leaving it out, at will. It’s a beautiful album.

Singer/songwriter Rodney Crowell takes an unflinching look at his rough-and-tumble Texas upbringing with his new album, “The Houston Kid,” due Feb. 13 on Sugar Hill Records.

# Rodney Crowell Looks Back On ‘Houston Kid’
### Billboard Staff
#### More Stories by Billboard
The rootsy, acoustic-rock record relies heavily on imagery-often unpleasant-conjured from Crowell’s memories of his youth on the wrong side of the tracks in Houston. “For the most part, this record is autobiographical,” the artist says. “At some point, the story of ‘The Houston Kid’ takes my experiences from 6 to 15 years old, and it sort of cross-pollinates with other kids in my neighborhood. It fuses their experiences with what was going on in my life.”
The picture isn’t always pretty. Songs like “Telephone Road,” “The Rock Of My Soul,” and “Topsy Turvy” paint a picture of exuberant survival instincts put in use by an environment of alcohol and abuse.
Stylistically, the set leans more toward Bruce Springsteen’s “The Ghost Of Tom Joad” than Crowell’s past, more commercial efforts. Yet in spite of the grittiness, Crowell maintains an affection for those times. “Even in the really dark years, I was having fun,” he says. “My spirit wasn’t killed by the abuse that was going on.”
While “Telephone Road” is a colorful homage to the ice houses and honky-tonks of East Houston, the smoldering “Rock Of My Soul” addresses tougher themes-mainly, domestic violence-with lyrics like “I’m a firsthand witness to an age-old crime/A man who hits a woman isn’t worth a dime.”
Crowell says the Tom Petty-esque “Why Don’t We Talk About It” takes the point of view that “the Houston Kid grows up.” Such lyrics as “Guess my reputation says I’m flaky/Hey, my whole situation’s kinda shaky” bring to mind Crowell’s sometimes tenuous relationship with the Nashville music business.
“Have I felt misunderstood by Music Row at times?” he asks. “Of course.”

It’s ironic. In 1988, the country-music singer/songwriter Rodney Crowell released his fifth album, _Diamonds and Dirt_, which set a record, so to speak. No country album had ever spawned five #1 singles. _Diamonds and Dirt_ did, elevating the 38-year-old, who had written hits for artists from Waylon Jennings to Crystal Gayle and spent three years playing rhythm guitar in Emmylou Harris’s band, to the upper reaches of country-music stardom.
Artistically, the songs were nothing special, but with Columbia Records’ hitmaking machinery propelling them, they were catchy enough to top _Billboard_’s country chart. One, the driving, uptempo, and funny “She’s Crazy For Leaving,” was a legitimate #1. The rest were well-produced, well-marketed pablum.
Hence the irony I’ve alluded to. Crowell released his 10th album, _The Houston Kid_, in 2001, on little Sugar Hill Records (not to be confused with rap’s Sugar Hill). Evidently, the album had too little commercial potential to warrant a major label’s attention. No songs from _The Houston Kid_ charted. Yet critics—including this one, who reviewed the record for _Entertainment Weekly—_ almost unanimously agreed that this album was the artist’s finest piece of work yet, leaving Crowell’s major-label releases in the dirt.
One realizes on a first listen that _The Houston Kid_ is not the usual collection of 10 or so widely disparate songs. It’s what is known in the record business as a concept album, in this case an autobiographical song cycle, although, as anyone familiar with the contours of Crowell’s life recognized, _The Houston Kid_ made little attempt to stick to the facts. It was a work of imagination more or less based on the facts, and it was funny, sad, angry, ironic and deeply moving.
Crowell grew up on the wrong side of the tracks: run-down East Houston in the 1950s. Raunchy or not, the neighborhood had plenty to offer a lively kid with an appetite for fun and an imagination, as the opening song, “Telephone Road,” makes clear:
Video 11
texts.1:
“The Rock of My Soul,” which follows, is an unsparing portrait of the narrator’s parents, further establishing the harsh economic and emotional circumstances in which Crowell, or his persona, was raised, and the boy’s determination to avoid his mama and daddy’s fate.
Video 12
By the fifth song, “Wandering Boy,” the story has jumped ahead a number of years and taken a sharp turn onto an entirely imaginary road, about the brother Crowell never had (he was an only child), who, moreover, is dying of AIDs, and whom the protagonist urges to come home, where he can die comforted by a brother’s love. “Wandering Boy” is an unsentimental heartbreaker, strong evidence of Crowell’s growth as a writer since those late-‘80s Columbia hits.
Crowell had married into country-music royalty in 1979, tying the knot with Johnny Cash’s daughter Rosanne, a star herself. The couple divorced in 1992 but remained on friendly enough terms for Rosanne’s father not merely to agree to sing on _The Houston Kid_’s sixth song, “I Walk the Line (Revisited)”, but to sing a _rewritten version_ of “I Walk the Line”, allowing his ex-son-in-law to “paint a mustache on John’s Mona Lisa," as Crowell later put it. Cash good-naturedly throws himself into the spirit of Crowell’s brazen rewrite, singing the hell out of it. “I Walk the Line (Revisited)” is not only hilarious, but captures (most likely imagines) a major moment in the childhood of a future country-music singer.
Video 13
“Highway 17,” which immediately follows Crowell’s act of _lèse-majesté,_ packs quite an emotional wallop. The song’s narrator, presumably the Crowell character’s semi-hoodlum of a father, is a career thief with what he considers a master plan, who suffers agonizingly at what was to be his moment of triumph. “Highway 17” may be _The Houston Kid_’s most imaginative and visceral song. Here’s Crowell singing it live in 2010.
Video 14
texts.2:
Four songs follow “Highway 17,” all of them strong, especially “U Don’t Know How Much I Hate You,” with its jolting last-line confession. To these ears, the song could easily have been inspired by Crowell’s and Cash’s divorce. Even if it was written after Crowell’s 1998 remarriage, resentment lingers.
In the final song of the 11-song cycle, the narrator, amid peaceful circumstances at last, looks back on his melodrama of a life, forgives his now-departed parents their transgressions, and counts his blessings. The song is titled “Love is All I Need.” Here’s a performance from 2009.
Video 15
More than a dozen Crowell albums, including collaborations—two with his old boss Emmylou Harris—have followed _The Houston Kid._ There are many I haven’t listened to. All I can say is that at the time it was released, it was by far Crowell’s best piece of work. He has since collected many awards, both for lifetime achievement and individual songs and albums. Neither _The Houston Kid_ nor any of its songs were nominated for, let alone won, anything.
In 2011, Crowell published a memoir, _Chinaberry Sidewalks_ (Vintage), its title taken from the chinaberry branches with which Addie Cauzette Crowell regularly whipped her son. _Chinaberry Sidewalks_ makes it clear how many liberties Crowell took with the truth in _The Houston Kid_. Which, of course, detracts not a bit from the album’s achievement. _Chinaberry Sidewalks_ is a work of non-fiction (and a well-written one at that). _The Houston Kid_ is an imaginative reworking of Crowell’s past, sticking to fact when it serves his purposes, and altering it, or leaving it out, at will. It’s a beautiful album.

# Rodney Crowell Looks Back On ‘Houston Kid’
### Billboard Staff
#### More Stories by Billboard
The rootsy, acoustic-rock record relies heavily on imagery-often unpleasant-conjured from Crowell’s memories of his youth on the wrong side of the tracks in Houston. “For the most part, this record is autobiographical,” the artist says. “At some point, the story of ‘The Houston Kid’ takes my experiences from 6 to 15 years old, and it sort of cross-pollinates with other kids in my neighborhood. It fuses their experiences with what was going on in my life.”
The picture isn’t always pretty. Songs like “Telephone Road,” “The Rock Of My Soul,” and “Topsy Turvy” paint a picture of exuberant survival instincts put in use by an environment of alcohol and abuse.
Stylistically, the set leans more toward Bruce Springsteen’s “The Ghost Of Tom Joad” than Crowell’s past, more commercial efforts. Yet in spite of the grittiness, Crowell maintains an affection for those times. “Even in the really dark years, I was having fun,” he says. “My spirit wasn’t killed by the abuse that was going on.”
While “Telephone Road” is a colorful homage to the ice houses and honky-tonks of East Houston, the smoldering “Rock Of My Soul” addresses tougher themes-mainly, domestic violence-with lyrics like “I’m a firsthand witness to an age-old crime/A man who hits a woman isn’t worth a dime.”
Crowell says the Tom Petty-esque “Why Don’t We Talk About It” takes the point of view that “the Houston Kid grows up.” Such lyrics as “Guess my reputation says I’m flaky/Hey, my whole situation’s kinda shaky” bring to mind Crowell’s sometimes tenuous relationship with the Nashville music business.
“Have I felt misunderstood by Music Row at times?” he asks. “Of course.”

One, the driving, uptempo, and funny “She’s Crazy For Leaving,” was a legitimate #1. The rest were well-produced, well-marketed pablum.
Hence the irony I’ve alluded to. Crowell released his 10th album, _The Houston Kid_, in 2001, on little Sugar Hill Records (not to be confused with rap’s Sugar Hill). Evidently, the album had too little commercial potential to warrant a major label’s attention. No songs from _The Houston Kid_ charted. Yet critics—including this one, who reviewed the record for _Entertainment Weekly—_ almost unanimously agreed that this album was the artist’s finest piece of work yet, leaving Crowell’s major-label releases in the dirt.
One realizes on a first listen that _The Houston Kid_ is not the usual collection of 10 or so widely disparate songs. It’s what is known in the record business as a concept album, in this case an autobiographical song cycle, although, as anyone familiar with the contours of Crowell’s life recognized, _The Houston Kid_ made little attempt to stick to the facts. It was a work of imagination more or less based on the facts, and it was funny, sad, angry, ironic and deeply moving.
Crowell grew up on the wrong side of the tracks: run-down East Houston in the 1950s. Raunchy or not, the neighborhood had plenty to offer a lively kid with an appetite for fun and an imagination, as the opening song, “Telephone Road,” makes clear:
Video 11

“The Rock of My Soul,” which follows, is an unsparing portrait of the narrator’s parents, further establishing the harsh economic and emotional circumstances in which Crowell, or his persona, was raised, and the boy’s determination to avoid his mama and daddy’s fate.
Video 12
By the fifth song, “Wandering Boy,” the story has jumped ahead a number of years and taken a sharp turn onto an entirely imaginary road, about the brother Crowell never had (he was an only child), who, moreover, is dying of AIDs, and whom the protagonist urges to come home, where he can die comforted by a brother’s love. “Wandering Boy” is an unsentimental heartbreaker, strong evidence of Crowell’s growth as a writer since those late-‘80s Columbia hits.
Crowell had married into country-music royalty in 1979, tying the knot with Johnny Cash’s daughter Rosanne, a star herself. The couple divorced in 1992 but remained on friendly enough terms for Rosanne’s father not merely to agree to sing on _The Houston Kid_’s sixth song, “I Walk the Line (Revisited)”, but to sing a _rewritten version_ of “I Walk the Line”, allowing his ex-son-in-law to “paint a mustache on John’s Mona Lisa," as Crowell later put it. Cash good-naturedly throws himself into the spirit of Crowell’s brazen rewrite, singing the hell out of it. “I Walk the Line (Revisited)” is not only hilarious, but captures (most likely imagines) a major moment in the childhood of a future country-music singer.
Video 13
“Highway 17,” which immediately follows Crowell’s act of _lèse-majesté,_ packs quite an emotional wallop. The song’s narrator, presumably the Crowell character’s semi-hoodlum of a father, is a career thief with what he considers a master plan, who suffers agonizingly at what was to be his moment of triumph. “Highway 17” may be _The Houston Kid_’s most imaginative and visceral song. Here’s Crowell singing it live in 2010.
Video 14

Four songs follow “Highway 17,” all of them strong, especially “U Don’t Know How Much I Hate You,” with its jolting last-line confession. To these ears, the song could easily have been inspired by Crowell’s and Cash’s divorce. Even if it was written after Crowell’s 1998 remarriage, resentment lingers.
In the final song of the 11-song cycle, the narrator, amid peaceful circumstances at last, looks back on his melodrama of a life, forgives his now-departed parents their transgressions, and counts his blessings. The song is titled “Love is All I Need.” Here’s a performance from 2009.
Video 15
More than a dozen Crowell albums, including collaborations—two with his old boss Emmylou Harris—have followed _The Houston Kid._ There are many I haven’t listened to. All I can say is that at the time it was released, it was by far Crowell’s best piece of work. He has since collected many awards, both for lifetime achievement and individual songs and albums. Neither _The Houston Kid_ nor any of its songs were nominated for, let alone won, anything.
In 2011, Crowell published a memoir, _Chinaberry Sidewalks_ (Vintage), its title taken from the chinaberry branches with which Addie Cauzette Crowell regularly whipped her son. _Chinaberry Sidewalks_ makes it clear how many liberties Crowell took with the truth in _The Houston Kid_. Which, of course, detracts not a bit from the album’s achievement. _Chinaberry Sidewalks_ is a work of non-fiction (and a well-written one at that). _The Houston Kid_ is an imaginative reworking of Crowell’s past, sticking to fact when it serves his purposes, and altering it, or leaving it out, at will. It’s a beautiful album.

### Billboard Staff

The rootsy, acoustic-rock record relies heavily on imagery-often unpleasant-conjured from Crowell’s memories of his youth on the wrong side of the tracks in Houston. “For the most part, this record is autobiographical,” the artist says. “At some point, the story of ‘The Houston Kid’ takes my experiences from 6 to 15 years old, and it sort of cross-pollinates with other kids in my neighborhood. It fuses their experiences with what was going on in my life.”
The picture isn’t always pretty. Songs like “Telephone Road,” “The Rock Of My Soul,” and “Topsy Turvy” paint a picture of exuberant survival instincts put in use by an environment of alcohol and abuse.
Stylistically, the set leans more toward Bruce Springsteen’s “The Ghost Of Tom Joad” than Crowell’s past, more commercial efforts. Yet in spite of the grittiness, Crowell maintains an affection for those times. “Even in the really dark years, I was having fun,” he says. “My spirit wasn’t killed by the abuse that was going on.”
While “Telephone Road” is a colorful homage to the ice houses and honky-tonks of East Houston, the smoldering “Rock Of My Soul” addresses tougher themes-mainly, domestic violence-with lyrics like “I’m a firsthand witness to an age-old crime/A man who hits a woman isn’t worth a dime.”
Crowell says the Tom Petty-esque “Why Don’t We Talk About It” takes the point of view that “the Houston Kid grows up.” Such lyrics as “Guess my reputation says I’m flaky/Hey, my whole situation’s kinda shaky” bring to mind Crowell’s sometimes tenuous relationship with the Nashville music business.
“Have I felt misunderstood by Music Row at times?” he asks. “Of course.”
